items.rationale: The difference is who owns the control flow: in a workflow, predefined code paths decide the steps and the order; in an agent, the model decides its own next step and tool use. Tools (a), the number of model calls (b) and whether a model is present (d) do not separate them, since workflows can call a model many times and use tools.

The program fixes the order of the steps and the model only does text work inside two of them, so it is a workflow. Having a model in the sequence (b) or a tool in it (c) does not make a system an agent; the model would have to choose the steps. The count of model calls (d) is not the test.
The agent makes 8 - 3 = 5 extra calls per request: 5 x $0.01 = $0.05 more per request, and 500 x $0.05 = $25.

Booking has known steps in a known order, so code can own the flow and the result is predictable and cheap. The other options are open-ended or unpredictable tasks where the needed steps vary by case, which is where an agent's flexibility pays off.

accepted: the flexibility to handle unplanned cases
items.rationale: A fixed workflow follows only the paths its code lists, so it cannot adapt to cases or steps nobody planned for; that is what it trades for predictability and lower cost.

An agent is worth its extra cost and unpredictability when the steps cannot be fixed in advance, so the model must choose them. Interest in agents (a) is not a requirement, and a lower cost (c) or identical steps every time (d) are reasons to keep the workflow.
